title: The Lutein and Zeaxanthin in Pregnancy Study 2
official: The Lutein and Zeaxanthin in Pregnancy Study 2 (L - ZIP II); Prenatal Carotenoid Supplement in in High-Risk Pregnancies
summary: This study is designed to test the hypotheses that (1) the third trimester of pregnancy is a period of maternal systemic and ocular carotenoid depletion; (2) prenatal supplementation with 10.0 milligrams of lutein and 2.0 milligrams of zeaxanthin will have significant effects on ocular and systemic biomarkers of maternal and infant carotenoid status relative to a matched, standard-of-care prenatal supplement without added lutein and zeaxanthin, and (3) mothers and infants assigned to the lutein + zeaxanthin group will have fewer adverse outcomes of high-risk pregnancies. Mothers will be enrolled in the study during their first trimester, and will take the study carotenoid or control supplements for 6 to 8 months. The final study outcome measurements of mothers and infants will be completed within two weeks of the baby's birth.

interventions.name: Softgel active ingredients: Lutein 10 mg and Zeaxanthin 2 mg in safflower oil

criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Pregnant women with high- and low-risk pregnancies, of all races and ethnicities, 18 years of age or older who plan to deliver their baby at the KNUST Hospital will be offered enrollment prior to 14 weeks of gestation. Women who are planning delivery by either vaginal or Cesarean section will be included.

High-risk pregnancy criteria and rationale for inclusion:

* History of pre-eclampsia (PE) - Endothelial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress contribute to the pathogenesis of PE. Women with a history of PE are at significantly increased risk of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies. Hence, they represent a clinically meaningful high-risk group to evaluate whether prenatal carotenoid supplementation could reduce the oxidative burden and improve outcomes.
* History of preterm delivery of a viable child (\<37 weeks 0 days gestational age (GA)) or history of delivery of a child who was small for gestational age (SGA; \< 10th percentile) - Preterm delivery and pregnancies with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) are associated with increased intrauterine inflammation and heightened oxidative stress, resulting in premature rupture of membranes, placental dysfunction, early labor, and infants who are SGA at birth.
* Current hypertension requiring medication - These individuals are prone to having pre-eclampsia, preterm delivery, and IUGR that result from placental perfusion impairment.
* Diabetes mellitus - Pregestational diabetes (diet-controlled or on current medication) is linked with increased oxidative stress, chronic low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction.
* High body mass index (BMI) (\>35 kg/m2) at enrollment - To ensure recruitment of a metabolically high-risk population while avoiding over-inclusion of individuals with BMI levels often considered borderline or common in the general U.S. population, we will initially set the BMI inclusion threshold at ≥35 kg/m². This cutoff more accurately reflects Class II obesity, which is strongly associated with oxidative stress and adverse pregnancy outcomes relevant to our study aims.
* Mothers with potential nutritional depletion prior to the onset of pregnancy due to low BMI (\<18 kg/m2) or five or more previous deliveries at \>20 weeks GA - Low BMI suggests potential malnutrition or underlying health conditions that may influence oxidative stress or pregnancy outcomes. Grand multiparity, defined as five or more live or stillbirths after 20 weeks of gestation, could compromise her carotenoid stores and leave her at risk for carotenoid depletion in subsequent pregnancies.
* Advanced maternal age \>40 years of age - Although advanced maternal age as risk factor for adverse outcomes of pregnancy is officially set at ≥35 years of age by the ACOG , the risks of preeclampsia rise substantially beginning at age 40 to 5-10% from a baseline of 3-4% in the general population.
* Current tobacco use of \>0.5 pack per day at the time of enrollment - Active cigarette smoking of at least 1/2 pack per day (≥10 cigarettes) at the time of enrollment will be an inclusion criterion. This threshold identifies individuals with significant tobacco exposure, which is known to affect oxidative stress levels, carotenoid metabolism, and pregnancy outcomes.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Multifetal pregnancies will be excluded due to higher inherent risk of pre-term birth and challenges in statistical analysis.
* Individuals \<18 years old will be excluded due to physiological and psychological immaturity and because of ethical considerations surrounding informed consent for minors.
* Individuals who have regularly taken carotenoid supplements containing more than 0.5 mg of lutein and/or zeaxanthin daily in the six months will be excluded to avoid confounding baseline levels and to ensure a clear assessment of the intervention's effects.
* Individuals who use illicit drugs will be excluded to minimize confounding variable that could impact maternal and fetal health and interfere with study adherence.
* Individuals who have significant macular disease will be excluded. Macular disease alters retinal structure and function, interferes with accurate macular carotenoid assessment, and confounds macular pigment outcome interpretation.
